Anthropic hasn't published the exploit. Its disclosure policy gives developers 90 days to patch and a further 45 days before Anthropic discusses details beyond a public advisory. Red Hat's bulletin now says the bug could be exploited "to trigger remote code execution." By 5:15 PM CDT on October 31, 36 GitHub repositories referenced the CVE. Most describe themselves as audit or mitigation tooling, among them Ansible roles and a livepatch for AlmaLinux and Rocky Linux. At least six say they include a race trigger or a proof of concept for the use-after-free; the first was created at 7:22 PM on October 29, and the latest at 11:04 AM on October 31. The CVE isn't in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of 5:15 PM CDT. We haven't tested any public proof of concept, and we aren't linking them.

Updates to this post

We'll revise this post and mark it updated when any of these change: fixed kernels from Ubuntu or Red Hat, or AlmaLinux's production release; NVD's analysis; a KEV listing or any report of exploitation; the separate IPv6 fix.

October 31, 5:15 PM CDT: Red Hat raised its rating from Important (8.1) to Critical (9.8) on October 30 and published a mitigation in bulletin RHSB-2026-016, so we replaced its earlier rating and its "no mitigation" statement. Added the Go Security Team's notice that Go programs open MPTCP listeners by default, AlmaLinux's fixed kernels in testing, Amazon Linux's fixes for its remaining kernels, openSUSE Leap 16.0's fix, steps to turn off MPTCP, an iptables version of the interim rule, and the interim rule's limits with bridged container traffic and CIPSO. 36 GitHub repositories now reference the CVE. Ubuntu, Debian, Oracle, NVD's status, and KEV are unchanged, and the stable kernels released October 30 don't include the IPv6 follow-up. October 29, 8:00 PM CDT: Added Oracle Linux, fixed in its UEK kernels since October 16, and Amazon Linux, fixed in Amazon Linux 2023's 6.12 and 6.18 kernels and pending elsewhere. Eight GitHub repositories now reference the CVE, one describing a race trigger. Ubuntu, Red Hat, Debian, SUSE, NVD, and KEV are unchanged since 11:00 AM, and nothing was corrected. Get help

If the hard part is knowing which hosts, nodes, and appliances run which kernel, and which of them can reboot this week, our advisors can help plan it.

The bug is reachable through any listening TCP port, so it helps to know which ones the internet can see. Our free external audit checks the domains and public IPs you verify for exposed services, publicly visible software versions with known CVEs, TLS, email security, DNS, and HTTP headers.

It's the second Linux kernel fix this month that only takes effect after a reboot. The other, Fragnesia, is being chained with PHP2Shell to get root.

item.title: HackerTube: YouTube built from videos recommended by HN
item.description:
HackerTube

It was Friday night at 11pm, I was tired, I went to YouTube to watch something and realized that I was looking at an enshittified wall of slop. Insanely exaggerated thumbnails, dumb recommendations of the same tired topics, truly terrible idiocracy-grade content. I'm sure this algorithm works well for the median person on the internet, but it definitely does not work for me. So this morning (Saturday) I took a hold of my Opus 5.5 and gave it the task: Let's write our own YouTube clone based on whatever videos have been recommended on Hacker News. And Opus came back with: hackertube.org!

Opus downloaded all comments of HackerNews, filtered them down, ran Sonnet over them in a workflow, got rid of spam and low grade content, and narrowed them down to just 40K comments recommending a YouTube video. In total, we get 6,454 YouTube videos that have been recommended by a few people on HN from 2007-2026 across 150 topics. Then we wrap it up in a YouTube UI, get a domain, push to a VPS, secure, harden, optimize and voila!

HackerTube:

Contains quality content Uses the 50% thumbnail instead of the uploaded thumbnail Custom and good ForYou recommendations without any user accounts, storing state in local browser session Keyboard shortcuts Export of the site's data available to give to your agent to easily create your own version

This takes ~2 hours now. I can breathe again. Thank you Opus 5.5 <3.

item.title: Surviving "The Graduate"
item.description:
When I went down to the pool at the Chateau Marmont, it seemed like everyone knew each other and was having fun in the sun.

I had been staying with my parents in L.A., shooting “The Graduate,” but my father was driving me crazy. Every day, I’d get home from the set, and he’d grill me, wanting to know every detail of what happened. And he’d be very critical: Why did you do that? That’s not the way to do it. I lasted maybe five days, and then I couldn’t take it anymore. I was trapped in the house where I’d grown up, totally alienated by the previous generation, just like my character. So I’d moved to the hotel where the cast and crew were staying.

Out by the pool, it was like a cabana party on Mount Olympus: the people looked like golden gods among the palm trees. I felt immediately uncomfortable, unworthy. Here I was, playing a starring role in a movie by Mike Nichols, who was the director of the moment, but I felt like I had no right to be there.

The shoot went on for months. Mike was in no rush; he had all the time and money he wanted. But I never went down to the pool again.

“The Graduate” exacerbated all my insecurities from the start. When my agent said that Mike was interested in me, I didn’t even want to try out for the part. I had read the Charles Webb novel that Mike was adapting, and it was obvious that I was all wrong for Benjamin. A track star and straight-A student, the head of the debate team—this was an affluent, all-American kid, whose surname was “Braddock.” Why would you cast a person who looks as ethnic as I do to play the ultimate Wasp? It made absolutely no sense.

It was impossible to be unimpressed by Mike, though. His first film, “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?,” had just been nominated for thirteen Academy Awards, including Best Directing and Best Picture. I’d enjoyed his version of “Barefoot in the Park” on Broadway, and I loved the comedy routines he’d done with Elaine May. Still—me, playing a six-foot gentile? I had to draw the line somewhere.

“I hear you don’t think you’re right for the part,” Mike said on the phone. “So who is right for it?”

There happened to be a copy of Time on the coffee table in front of me; on the cover was a sketch of a handsome, blond, athletic fellow meant to represent Americans “Twenty-five and Under.” “The guy on the cover of Time,” I said.

“You’re saying you’re not right for it because you’re Jewish,” Mike said.

“Well, because Benjamin’s so not Jewish.”

There was a pause. Then Mike said, “Maybe he’s Jewish inside.”

By that time, they’d been trying to cast the part for almost two years. “Robert Redford and Candice Bergen, the ideal couple—that’s what we were thinking,” Buck Henry, the film’s co-screenwriter, said about casting Benjamin and his love interest, Elaine. But they’d already seen Redford—and pretty much everyone else—by the time they got around to me and Katharine Ross. Nothing had clicked. I still maintain that if I’d read for them at the beginning of their search, instead of at the bitter end, I never would have got the part.

The irony is that I was just starting to become successful in theatre, the world I’d inhabited for almost a decade. I was in “Eh?” Off Broadway, and I was having a great experience: lots of laughs, standing ovations almost nightly, my face on the cover of the Arts section of the Times. I was finally making a living doing what I loved. It was as if I’d been hiking up a mountain and, just when I could finally see the summit, here comes Mike in a helicopter, offering me a ride to a different peak.

Hollywood had never been my endgame. As far as I was concerned, the studios kept beautiful people imprisoned in seven-year contracts. I wasn’t beautiful, and I didn’t want to be trapped. To be honest, I looked down on American movies, compared with theatre. When it came to breakthrough cinema, the kind made in Europe by greats like Truffaut, Buñuel, Antonioni, and Godard, Hollywood had yet to see the light.

My agent convinced me that I should screen-test for Mike, despite my reservations. I told my castmates in “Eh?” not to worry; I was sure they wouldn’t need to replace me. Then I walked to my neighbor on Eleventh Street, Mel Brooks, who’d suggested that I play a small part in “The Producers.” I called up to his window: “They’re flying me out to audition for a Mike Nichols movie.”

“What part?” he asked.

“The lead,” I told him.

“Good luck!” he said, suppressing a laugh. “Keep me posted!”

I had to learn ten pages in less than forty-eight hours. I stayed up the entire night running lines; by the time I landed in Los Angeles, I hadn’t slept in two days. Mike’s office was a series of palatial rooms with high ceilings, and in my memory it included a bar, which is where I first saw him. “Oh, hi, would you like a drink?” he said. He was always so casual, almost seductive. Then they brought in Katharine Ross, who was outrageously beautiful. I felt foolish, like I had to apologize to her for looking like I did.

They took us to get our makeup done in a long room with rows of upholstered chairs. Today, you get made up in a trailer, without a trace of glamour, but this room was a remnant of Old Hollywood. It seemed likely that Betty Grable’s ass had been on the chair before mine.

They had these famous makeup artists, the Westmores—six brothers who’d learned their trade from their father. I can’t remember how many of them were there that day, but they were at it for hours. And it’s not like I was getting prosthetics or a toupee. It took them that long just to do something with what little I offered.

Mike came in, watched them for a while, and looked at my face in the mirror. Quietly, in his singsong voice, he said, “Can’t you do something with his eyebrows?” Bobby Duvall always said that I had only one. They started plucking me to make two.

Then Mike said that my neck looked too thick, so they put me in a turtleneck. But he was still unhappy with what he was seeing. (I, too, was increasingly unhappy.) Mike sounded almost innocent when he asked the Westmores, “Now, what are we going to do about the nose?”

I remember thinking, They’re trying to take the Jew off my face, and it ain’t going to happen. All I wanted to do was go home, to ethnic New York, where I belonged. I knew I was no leading man. I knew my place.

The scene I did with Katharine was endless. Both of us kept screwing up because—for God knows what reason—Mike wanted to shoot a ten-minute scene in one take. At one point, he took me aside and said, “Why are you nervous? This isn’t a play; the curtain’s not opening. It’s not a movie. It won’t go any farther than this room. So just relax!” I felt that he understood completely, and I thanked him and shook his hand. It was so slippery with sweat that it literally slid out of mine. That’s when I realized that he was more anxious than I was, and this did not put me at ease.

It wasn’t just paranoia: everyone thought I was wrong for the part. “I looked at it, and it was just this ugly boy playing the part, and I thought, Ugh,” the film’s editor, Sam O’Steen, later said of my screen test. People imagined the Braddocks as prototypical California gentiles. “All blonde, all healthy,” Buck Henry said. “A family of surfboards is what we called them. And here comes Dustin: clearly not a surfboard.” To save the film, they hoped Benjamin’s parents might be played by Ronald Reagan and Doris Day. “We immediately rationalized it: he’s a genetic throwback,” Buck continued. “Doris Day and Ronald Reagan have had this mutt.”

I was so relieved when we finished the screen test. I couldn’t wait to get out of there. As I was thanking the propman, a few subway tokens dropped out of my pocket. He very nicely picked them up, then said, “Here, kid, you’re gonna need these.”

Soon after I got home to New York, my agent told me to call Mike at nine o’clock on Sunday morning. It was snowing out, and I was going uptown to my girlfriend’s apartment for breakfast. Obviously, the agent meant Pacific time, but I was such an anxious wreck that I didn’t think it through. When I got to my girlfriend’s place, I called Mike at precisely 9 A.M. New York time and woke him up.

I mumbled an apology. There was a long silence. “Well,” Mike said, “you got it.”

Stunned is too weak a word. Mike had apparently seen something in the footage. “He had this thing I’d only seen in Elizabeth Taylor, and that I’d certainly not seen in any of the other tests,” he later told his biographer, Mark Harris. “That secret. That deal with Technicolor where you do nothing and it turns out you were doing everything. He was compelling and hilarious and impassive. It was startling. That’s what a great movie actor does. They don’t know how they do it, and I don’t know how they do it, but the difference is shocking.”

I hung up the phone feeling like I’d been hit in the head. I looked at my girlfriend, who was holding a spatula, making our breakfast. “I got it,” I told her.

“I knew you would,” she said.

We had three weeks of rehearsal, which was unheard of for a film—a testament to just how revered Mike was, how much leverage he had in the industry.

“Don’t try to do a character, don’t try to be funny,” he told us. “Start from zero.” Mike took me back to my adolescence—my acne, my barely suppressed horniness. He asked me if I thought Benjamin Braddock was a virgin. I said no, but that I didn’t think he’d ever screwed his mother’s friend before, either. (He liked that response.)

Mike was completely open and unusually perceptive. I struggled, for instance, with the scene in the hotel lobby when Benjamin is registering for the room where he will have his first illicit encounter with Mrs. Robinson, the seductive, alienated housewife played by Anne Bancroft. Mike asked me all kinds of questions: What was it like when I lost my virginity? When had I experienced sexual shame? I told him that I could never bring myself to buy rubbers from a female pharmacist—if I was at the register and a woman appeared behind the counter, I had to make a break for it. Mike told me to think of the hotel clerk (played, to hilarious effect, by Buck Henry) as a woman pharmacist. It was such a useful piece of direction, such a helpful way of working.

Mike also asked me if I had a role model as a kid. I told him it was my brother Ronny. He had me try a scene as Ronny, who I could imitate perfectly; I used to pretend I was him when girls called him, hoping to see how long I could keep them on the phone. Then Mike asked me if Ronny ever got uptight, and he absolutely did. “Try it again, as your brother, uptight,” Mike said. So I did what Ronny did whenever he was nervous: I held my breath. Finally, Mike said, “Now forget all that and just do the scene.”

This time, I still held my breath a lot, but I also let out a little squeak periodically. Mike liked it so much he put in a few extra squeaks in the final edit. You can hear them throughout “The Graduate,” like gas escaping from Benjamin Braddock, who is a balloon of tension.

Mike was so wonderful during rehearsal that it was shocking, destabilizing, when we started shooting the film and he was an entirely different person. We weren’t allowed to see any dailies—I later found out it was because Mike didn’t want Anne Bancroft to see the way they were lighting her. (She was only thirty-five, and I was about to turn thirty; Mike had to make that five-year age gap look more like fifteen.) So we had nothing to go on but Mike’s mood, which was frequently sour.

I often felt that I was about to be fired. When we were shooting some of the film’s most famous sequences, I remember thinking, I have no fucking idea what I’m doing. The first scene that we shot featured Benjamin in front of a fish tank in his room, where he’s escaped from a party his parents have thrown to celebrate his college graduation. I just sat there on the bed while Mike told me, “O.K., look at the fish. Now look down. Move toward the fish.” We probably spent a whole day on it, and not for one second did I have a handle on what I was meant to be conveying or how to go about it.

I did make Mike laugh sometimes, and those were moments of great relief for me. When we started working on Benjamin and Mrs. Robinson’s first scene in the hotel room, I did what I’d done when I had my “first feel” as a teen-ager: I awkwardly and abruptly put my hand on Anne’s bra-covered breast, with absolutely no finesse or passion, without even making eye contact with her. Anne’s response was incredible: without missing a beat, she looked down at the sweater in her hands, noticed a stain, and paid it all of her attention, rubbing the fabric together and fussing with it, while I continued to hold her breast in my paw like a paralyzed animal.

It was so funny that I had to walk away, trying to avoid bursting into laughter. That was the worst thing you could do: break character. I started knocking my head against the wall in an attempt to collect myself. Don’t break! Don’t break! Mike interpreted it as an artistic choice, and it cracked him up. When Mike was laughing, I felt he loved the character I was trying to create. It was the only time I knew I was doing something he was happy with.

But his mood would shift dramatically. I don’t remember the scene, but I will never forget Mike’s acid voice saying to me, after one take: “What were you doing?”

I tried to defend myself: I’d been taught that to give your character depth, you don’t play the text—you play the subtext, which can sometimes be the opposite of the text.

“Well, do me a favor,” Mike said. “The next time you get a thought, do the opposite of that.”

This is the kind of comment that kept me in a state of constant anxiety. And it wasn’t just my own experience. When we shot a scene in which Benjamin drags Elaine, Mrs. Robinson’s daughter, to a strip club for their first date, Mike overheard Robert Surtees, the cinematographer, say something to the crew. Surtees was a mentor to Mike, the man who taught him all about the possibilities of light and filmmaking. “I said something snotty, as I often did, to the crew,” Mike recalled later. “And Surtees—I heard him say to them, but it wasn’t for me—he said, ‘It’s O.K. It’s not much longer.’ I thought, Oh man. How could I have been such a shit that this man that I revere feels that way about me? But I was.”

Mike was irritable with everyone, but with me a certain sadism seemed to creep in. There was a scene in which Katharine Ross had to slap me, and he made us do twenty-seven takes. The scene has Benjamin run into Elaine’s room, soaking wet from the rain, to tell her that he’s had an affair with an older woman; within seconds, Elaine realizes the woman is her mother. Mike just kept telling Katharine to hit me, to hit me harder. Katharine worried she would hurt me, and I told her, “I’m O.K. Just don’t hit my ear.” Unfortunately, she missed a few times. I was dizzy by the end of that day, and Mike didn’t even use the slap in the film.

The next day, we shot an underwater scene in the pool: Benjamin is being forced to try the scuba suit his father has bought for him. The scene was meant to symbolize the way that Benjamin’s parents gave their children material things instead of love. Mike didn’t want me to keep popping up out of the water, so I had to hold myself down: if you watch the movie, you can see that one hand is behind me the whole time I’m underwater, because I’m holding on to the ladder behind me. When I came up for air after a few takes, there was blood trickling out of my ear. Between all the slapping during the previous day and all the water pressure at the bottom of the pool, I’d punctured an eardrum. (They sent me to the best ear doctor in Beverly Hills, and I remember him telling me, “The eardrum is like a pie: you have a slice of pie missing.”)

By summer, we were shooting in La Verne, California. We got there the week of the Six-Day War—we all thought the world was going to end. The sound guy, Jack Solomon, heard about it on the radio, on the way to the set, and was so upset that he had to pull over to throw up. It was scorching hot. Anne Bancroft actually fainted when we were shooting a scene. She had to be resuscitated with oxygen, and we stopped shooting for a few days while she recovered.

I nearly passed out myself doing the scene where Benjamin, on his way to stop Elaine’s wedding, runs out of gas, has to ditch his Alfa Romeo, and sprints as fast as he can from the highway to the church. Mike could not be satisfied. I remember Sam O’Steen saying to him, “I don’t think Dusty can keep running in this heat.” But we did it over and over and over again, until I was absolutely trashed from exhaustion and dehydration. I remember lying down in the grass in front of the church because I thought I was going to lose consciousness.

It was a terrible experience making the movie that changed my life. The whole time, I felt Mike was angry at me, either because I was doing something wrong or because he had realized what everybody else already knew, that he had miscast the lead in his film. My friend Ulu Grosbard, a distinguished theatre director, came and visited toward the end of the shoot, and I told him, “If this is what it’s like doing a movie, I will never make another movie again for the rest of my life.” Ulu was taking Mike out to lunch, and I begged him to do some reporting: Was Mike regretting that he’d hired me? Ulu told me later that Mike had said, Yes, very much.

But apparently, after a few decades and some therapy, Mike arrived at a different explanation:

Mike lived in the Waspiest part of Connecticut. He collected antiques and cars and Arabian horses—the ultimate gentile status symbols. But he was very much a Jew, who’d fled Germany in 1939 and arrived in the United States, speaking not a word of English, at the age of seven. Born Mikhail Igor Peschkowsky, Mike always felt ugly. He had alopecia, and he was extremely self-conscious about his hairlessness. (He had a collection of incredible wigs that started with what his fantasy hair would look like freshly cut; on each successive day, the wig would be a little longer, until it was time for a “haircut.” Then he’d start the wig cycle again from the beginning.)

Eventually, he realized that he had made a self-portrait out of “The Graduate.” “My unconscious was making that movie,” he said once. He didn’t notice for years that, not long after his professional breakup with Elaine May—his partner in crime, his artistic collaborator since college—he made a movie in which the hero bangs against the glass wall of a church screaming, in anguish, “Elaine! Elaine! Elaine!” He was looking for an alter ego—that’s why Benjamin had taken years to cast, and maybe that’s why he was so hard on me. I was a stand-in, there to absorb Mike’s own self-loathing.

The first time that I saw “The Graduate” in a theatre was at a sneak preview on Eighty-sixth Street in Manhattan. My girlfriend and I sat in the back of the balcony, because I was very self-conscious and tense. My teeth were literally chattering when I saw the first shot, a closeup of my face.

At first, there was a weak reception. None of the humor seemed to be landing. I heard a spattering of laughter. Then more people joined in. About twenty minutes into the picture, the laughs started building. It was as though, little by little, the audience was figuring out where we were coming from. . . . There was a little more laughter, and then quite a lot more, and by the time Benjamin was screaming, “Elaine! Elaine! Elaine!” and she screams, “Ben!” and runs to him, the audience was standing up and screaming, too. It was like they had come to see a fight and had been waiting the whole time on the edge of their seats for this: the knockout.

I’ve been doing this for sixty years now. I don’t think I’ve ever seen anything like that since. I sat there, buried in my chair, and then I walked out with my girlfriend into the snow. ♦

This is drawn from “Look at Me.”

item.title: With 86% of the words, you might understand only 38% of an anime's lines
item.description:
With 86% of the words, you might understand only 38% of an anime's lines

Coverage tells you the percentage of spoken words you know, not how many lines you can follow. Measured in Frieren and seven other anime.

Say you want to watch Frieren, so you learn the 500 most common words in the show. A coverage calculator says that you now know 85.9% of the words spoken.

You make tea and press play. Here are three of the things you hear:

Blurred words fall outside the top 500. Hover or tap to reveal them.

By the third pause to look up a word, your tea has gone cold. With those 500 words, you know every word in 1,151 of the first 3,000 lines. That's 38.4% of them. The other 1,849 lines each contain at least one word you don't know.

Both numbers are true

Coverage is the number most learning sites quote. It's the percentage of spoken words that you know, so a particle spoken a thousand times counts a thousand times. The words at the very top of the Frieren list are all grammar pieces like の (of, 's) and は (topic marker), so the top 100 words alone give you 68.3% coverage. You'd follow only 8.5% of the lines.

Three figures describe the same 500 words:

What you're measuring Frieren, first 3,000 lines Words you know 500 of 2,448 different words (20.4%) Coverage, repeats included 85.9% Lines understood, every word known 38.4%

manga-kotoba builds its coverage tables this way. jpdb and jiten show a coverage figure too, though their help pages don't give the exact formula.

The gap between coverage and lines comes from line length. A Frieren line has 7 words on average. You need to know all seven to follow it. At 85.9% coverage, your chance of knowing a whole line is about 35%. That's 0.859 multiplied by itself seven times. It's close to the 38.4% of lines we measured.

Try it on a show you like

Thick line: lines understood in the chosen show. Dashed: coverage in that show. Pale lines: lines understood in the other seven. For each curve, we assumed you learn that show's most common words first.

All eight shows have this gap. Serial Experiments Lain reaches 95% coverage with the fewest words, 1,191. Even then, you'd follow only 77.5% of the lines.

Some shows need far fewer words than others

Serial Experiments Lain needs the fewest words of the eight: about 400 gets you half the lines. Jujutsu Kaisen needs 980.

Show Lines Episodes Different words Coverage at 500 Lines understood at 500 Words for half the lines Serial Experiments Lain 2,034 13 1,924 88.0% 55.9% 401 Dororo 3,000 13 2,431 85.2% 42.1% 633 Chainsaw Man 2,849 12 2,203 86.3% 41.1% 647 Frieren 3,000 12 2,448 85.9% 38.4% 730 Mob Psycho 100 3,000 8 2,795 82.4% 39.1% 749 Death Note 3,000 11 2,529 86.6% 36.0% 782 Hunter x Hunter (2011) 3,000 12 2,785 82.3% 34.6% 862 Jujutsu Kaisen 3,000 10 3,028 81.5% 32.7% 980

We capped every show at 3,000 lines so that a long show doesn't look harder for having more episodes. If a show gets harder later on, it looks easier here than it is.

Many of the lines you miss are only one word away

Back to Frieren. You missed 1,849 lines. Of those, 1,042 are missing a single word, which is 56.4%. Across all the shows, that figure runs from 50.2% to 63.9%.

Going from 500 to 1,000 words helps you far more than coverage suggests. Coverage only gains 6.5 points, because these new words don't come up often. Lines understood gain 22.1 points, because one new word is often the last one you needed to follow a line.

You can't fill these one-word gaps with a handful of words. Those 1,042 lines are missing 804 different words between them. The most you get from one word is 4 lines, from words like 後悔 (regret), 約束 (promise) and 収集 (collecting).

2,000 common Japanese words get you at most 38% of the lines

As a rough comparison, we tried the 2,000 most common words of general Japanese, from the wordfreq list. Those got you 23.4% to 37.6% of lines. We then tried each show's own top 2,000 words. They got 74.3% to 93.3% of lines. Serial Experiments Lain has fewer than 2,000 different words, so it isn't in that second range.

A show's top words can be unusual. Number 304 on the Frieren list is 生臭坊主, a monk who doesn't keep his vows, which is what the characters keep calling Heiter. Number 21 is 魔法 (magic), four places ahead of 私 (I).

A list from earlier episodes still does two-thirds of the job later on

Say you learn a show's top words from one season, then carry on to the next. We tested something close to this on the four shows with enough lines. We built each list from the first 3,000 lines, then tested it on the next 3,000. On Frieren's next 3,000 lines, the old list gets 22.3%, while a list built from those lines themselves gets 33.0%. The word 試験 (exam) appears only once in those first lines and 51 times after them, because the characters take a mage exam later on. Across those shows, the drop is 5.5 to 14.0 points.

Words with several meanings make these figures too high

Many words have several meanings, which linguists call polysemy. We counted a word as known whichever meaning a line uses. At 500 words, both of these Frieren lines count as understood: 手が震えています (my hands are shaking) and 手に取るように分かる (I can read it like a book). You could know 手 (hand) perfectly from the first line and still be lost in the second. Word for word, it says "as if taking it in your hand." We didn't measure how many lines have this problem. On this count alone, the lines-understood figures are too high.

How we did it The recipe Clean the subtitles by removing songs, formatting tags, anything in brackets and music notes. Split the text into sentence-sized lines. Remove duplicate lines. Split every line into words with Sudachi, a free Japanese tokenizer. We used SudachiPy 0.6.11 with SudachiDict-core 20260428 in split mode C. Our Python version was 3.13.7. Use each word's dictionary form, so 行った (went) and 行く (go) count as one word. Skip punctuation, numbers and anything Sudachi tags as a proper name. Skip fillers like シッ (shh) and ハハッ (ha ha). A sound only counts as filler when Sudachi tags it as an interjection, adverb or noun. We still count the grammar ending ん, which has a different tag. Particles and everyday replies like うん (yeah) still count as words. Drop lines with no words left, sort by episode and keep the first 3,000 lines. Count how often each word appears, then rank them. Break ties alphabetically. Treat the top N words as known. Coverage is known word occurrences divided by all word occurrences. Lines understood is the percentage of lines where every word is known. The whole thing in 29 lines of Python # pip install sudachipy sudachidict_core # lines.txt: one subtitle line per row, in episode order, songs and repeats removed # fillers.txt: your own list of sounds not to count, one per row from collections import Counter from sudachipy import Dictionary, SplitMode import re tok = Dictionary().create() fillers = set(open("fillers.txt", encoding="utf-8").read().split()) def words(line): out = [] for m in tok.tokenize(line, SplitMode.C): pos = m.part_of_speech() if pos[0] in ("補助記号", "空白", "記号"): continue # punctuation if pos[1] in ("固有名詞", "数詞"): continue # names, numbers if not re.search(r"[0-9A-Za-zぁ-ヿ一-鿿々]", m.surface()): continue if m.surface() in fillers and pos[0] in ("感動詞", "副詞", "名詞"): continue out.append(m.dictionary_form()) return out lines = [words(l.strip()) for l in open("lines.txt", encoding="utf-8")] lines = [l for l in lines if l][:3000] # the first 3,000 lines with a real word count = Counter(w for line in lines for w in line) known = {w for w, _ in sorted(count.items(), key=lambda x: (-x[1], x[0]))[:500]} coverage = sum(n for w, n in count.items() if w in known) / sum(count.values()) understood = sum(all(w in known for w in line) for line in lines) / len(lines) print(f"coverage: {coverage:.1%} lines understood: {understood:.1%}")

Run on our Frieren lines, this prints 85.9% and 38.4%. We don't store the unprocessed subtitle files. Your own subtitles and filler list will give you slightly different numbers.

All the numbers

Each cell shows coverage, then lines understood, at that many known words.

Show 100 words 250 words 500 words 1,000 words 2,000 words Serial Experiments Lain 70.8% / 20.2% 81.4% / 38.8% 88.0% / 55.9% 93.7% / 73.0% n/a Dororo 64.5% / 10.1% 76.6% / 24.6% 85.2% / 42.1% 92.0% / 63.1% 97.8% / 87.6% Chainsaw Man 66.0% / 9.4% 78.4% / 23.8% 86.3% / 41.1% 93.2% / 65.3% 98.9% / 93.3% Frieren 68.3% / 8.5% 78.7% / 22.5% 85.9% / 38.4% 92.4% / 60.5% 98.0% / 86.9% Mob Psycho 100 64.7% / 11.3% 75.1% / 25.4% 82.4% / 39.1% 89.5% / 58.0% 95.8% / 79.5% Death Note 67.3% / 6.9% 78.9% / 18.0% 86.6% / 36.0% 93.0% / 59.1% 98.0% / 84.6% Hunter x Hunter (2011) 63.0% / 9.0% 74.0% / 20.9% 82.3% / 34.6% 89.9% / 55.1% 96.3% / 79.6% Jujutsu Kaisen 63.7% / 9.5% 74.3% / 20.7% 81.5% / 32.7% 88.4% / 50.5% 94.8% / 74.3%

Known words needed to reach a given percentage of lines understood:

Show 25% of lines 50% 75% 90% Serial Experiments Lain 130 401 1,082 1,686 Dororo 254 633 1,429 2,101 Chainsaw Man 263 647 1,313 1,893 Frieren 283 730 1,491 2,111 Mob Psycho 100 241 749 1,775 2,458 Death Note 345 782 1,545 2,200 Hunter x Hunter (2011) 320 862 1,768 2,446 Jujutsu Kaisen 328 980 2,032 2,695
What could make this wrong "Understood" means you know every word. It ignores grammar, kanji readings, speaking speed and context. We assume you know exactly the show's most common words and haven't forgotten any. If you knew other words instead, or forgot some, these figures would be lower. You'd also need a list of the show's words before watching. Each different line counts once. In the show you'd hear stock lines like うん (yeah) again and again, which would likely raise lines understood. We didn't measure this. The lines come from each show's earliest episodes, with no episode skipped. Chainsaw Man and Serial Experiments Lain have fewer than 3,000 lines, so we used all of theirs. Fewer lines mean a higher score. At 500 words, the other shows score up to 4.8 points higher when cut to Lain's length. Serial Experiments Lain's subtitles are lower quality, so its figures are less reliable. Some subtitle files repeat a line in slightly different wording, and we only removed exact duplicates. Removing the close copies too changes lines understood at 500 words by at most 2.2 points. Deciding what counts as filler is a judgment call. If you count fillers as words, lines understood at 500 words differ by 2.7 points at most. The change goes in both directions because the lines we count shift. Counting forms as heard, so that 行った and 行く count separately, lowers lines understood by 5.3 to 7.7 points at 500 words. A word counts once however many meanings it has, which makes both coverage and lines understood too high. We have no count of which meaning each line uses. As a partial test, we counted a word separately for each part of speech Sudachi gives it, which lowers lines understood by 1.2 to 2.5 points at 500 words. That test only catches differences like noun against verb. Sudachi makes mistakes. It sometimes cuts a word into a fragment. It also treats some names as ordinary words: フリーレン (Frieren) is number 31 on her own list. Counting every word Sudachi doesn't recognize as known adds at most 0.6 points at 500 words.

learnfromx is a flashcard app that teaches Japanese from anime. Each card uses a line where you know everything except the one new word, which is why we started counting lines. The figures above count each word once, however many meanings it has. That wouldn't work in the app: knowing あれ as "that" doesn't help when someone says あれ？ (huh?). These are two separate cards. It doesn't catch every such word yet, we're working on it. During early access it offers one show, Hunter x Hunter.

News

Please try our Walkthrough for a preview of the steps involved when proofreading on this site.

Site Concept

Distributed Proofreaders provides a web-based method to ease the conversion of Public Domain books into e-books. By dividing the workload into individual pages, many volunteers can work on a book at the same time, which significantly speeds up the creation process.

During proofreading, volunteers are presented with a scanned page image and the corresponding OCR text on a single web page. This allows the text to be easily compared to the image, proofread, and sent back to the site. A second volunteer is then presented with the first volunteer's work and the same page image, verifies and corrects the work as necessary, and submits it back to the site. The book then similarly progresses through a third proofreading round and two formatting rounds using the same web interface.

Once all the pages have completed these steps, a post-processor carefully assembles them into an e-book, optionally makes it available to interested parties for 'smooth reading', and submits it to the Project Gutenberg archive.

How You Can Help Register with the site as a volunteerand/or Donate to the Distributed Proofreaders Foundation.

Registered volunteers may contribute to Distributed Proofreaders in several ways including proofreading, "smooth reading" pre-released e-books to check for errors, managing projects, providing content, or even helping develop improvements to the site. Volunteers may also join other members of our community in our forums to discuss these and many other topics.

Volunteering at Distributed Proofreaders

It's easy to volunteer at Distributed Proofreaders. Simply register as a volunteer. Once you've confirmed your registration by e-mail, you'll receive an introductory e-mail with basic instructions on how to log in and use the site. Then, you're ready to sign in and start learning to proofread or visit the smooth reading page to pick an e-book to read! Wherever you go, you'll find lots of information to help you get started. Please try our Walkthrough for a preview of the steps involved when proofreading on this site.

There is no commitment expected on this site beyond the understanding that you do your best. Spend as much or as little time as you like. We encourage you to proofread at least a page a day and/or smooth read a book as often as your time allows, but it's entirely up to you.

We hope you will join us in our mission of "preserving the literary history of the world in a freely available form for everyone to use."

We are unable to provide certification for any purpose that would require Distributed Proofreaders to track the number of hours spent volunteering, or to provide verification of a user's identity beyond that provided by their email address, or to certify that the volunteer personally performed the work. For these reasons, we cannot provide certification for court-ordered community service, programs operated by federal, state, or municipal governments, etc. For more information, please see this page.

Current Progress

These books have been processed through our site and posted to the Project Gutenberg archive.

These books are undergoing their final checks before being assembled into a completed e-book.

These books are currently being processed through our site; sign in and start helping!

Our community of proofreaders, project managers, developers, etc. is composed entirely of volunteers. 339 active users in the past twenty-four hours. 712 active users in the past 7 days. 1,253 active users in the past 30 days.

Questions or comments? Please contact us at dphelp@pgdp.net.

Mission

Distributed Proofreaders is dedicated to the preservation of written works that are in the Public Domain in the United States by converting them into high-quality, freely available digital transcriptions. This is accomplished through the efforts of a supportive community of volunteers. Distributed Proofreaders follows the principles of the American Library Association Freedom to Read statement.

History

Distributed Proofreaders was founded in 2000 by Charles Franks to support the digitization of Public Domain books. Originally conceived to assist Project Gutenberg (PG), Distributed Proofreaders (DP) is now the main source of PG e-books. In 2002, Distributed Proofreaders became an official PG site. In May 2006, Distributed Proofreaders became a separate legal entity and continues to maintain a strong relationship with PG.

item.title: An Italian farmer found some unknown seeds in his attic and planted them
item.description:
An Italian Farmer Found Some Unknown Seeds in His Attic and, With Nothing to Lose, Planted Them. The Result Was Almost Biblical When a seven-eared stem emerged from the ground, it seemed like a miracle. What Claudio Grossi had unearthed was an ancient grain that proved to be an answer to some modern problems

Sometime in the early 1990s, Claudio Grossi, a 40-year-old farmer in Parma, in northern Italy, was cleaning his attic when he turned up an old sack full of seeds that he couldn’t identify. The bag, he was sure, had been left by his late great-grandfather, who’d started the farmstead around 1915. Grossi had no idea how long the seeds had been sitting there, deprived of water, soil and sun. Dry and cracked, the kernels looked so old in the palm of his hand that he doubted anything would ever sprout from them. He carried the bag down the stairs, shook the seeds out into a pile of manure and then forgot about them.

To his surprise, the seeds soon sprouted a few different types of wheat. One was particularly striking: At six feet high, its plants were about twice as tall as commercial wheat. But the most remarkable feature came when it developed ears—the grain-studded parts at the top of the plant. All of the wheat types Grossi had previously seen grew only one such ear. But the tall wheat grew a full seven ears, always in the same pattern: a long one with six shorties bunched up around it like little fingers. Even the kernels themselves were bigger than those of average wheat. And unlike the typical pale-yellow wheat kernels, they came in a rainbow of colors—yellow, black, red, white and even green, sometimes all on the same stem. Grossi, a grain farmer his whole life, had never seen anything like it. “I thought it was a freak of nature,” he says. He couldn’t find a mention of it in agricultural books.

For Grossi, a practicing Catholic, the next insight came from a different book altogether. Leafing through a Bible at church one Sunday, he found a passage in the Book of Genesis describing a stalk with seven ears, in a dream that Joseph interprets for the Pharaoh: “And he slept and dreamed the second time: And, behold, seven ears of grain came up upon one stalk, rank and good. And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them. And the seven thin ears devoured the seven rank and full ears.” To Grossi, that sounded just like the mysterious crop in his manure pile.

“I connected the dots,” Grossi says. That grain must be really ancient, he thought. And if people were farming this odd-looking wheat in biblical times, why does no one today?

Back on his farm, Grossi harvested the grain, milled it into flour and baked a loaf of bread in his kitchen. Compared with commercial wheat, the dough didn’t rise well, but as the loaf sat in the oven, it filled the kitchen with a surprisingly nutty and delicious aroma. Once finished, it had a rich, satisfying taste. “You get these notes of sweetness that you can’t find in regular commercial flour,” he says.

Did you know? More miracles of grain in the Bible

In 2 Kings 4:42-44, Elisha multiplies 20 barley loaves in order to feed 100 men—anticipating Jesus’s “Feeding of the 5,000” in the gospels.

In 1 Kings 17:8-16, Elisha helps a widow at Zarephath to outlast a drought and famine with only a handful of flour and a little oil.

In Judges 7:9-15, a Midianite soldier recounts a dream in which a barley loaf tumbles into the camp and overturns a tent. Gideon, the judge and military leader, recognizes the dream as a sign that God will deliver the Midianites into Israel's hands.

In 2 Kings 4:38-41, during a famine, someone gathers wild gourds and cuts them into a pot of stew. The diners discover that the stew is dangerous and cry out to Elisha. He calls for flour and throws it into the pot—and the stew becomes miraculously safe to eat.

Grossi discovered it had other advantages: It was hardier and more self-sufficient than commercial varieties. It fared better during droughts, growing so tall that it overshadowed the weeds. It didn’t need fertilizer or herbicides. Indeed, it seemed so superior to its industrial cousins that he thought of it no longer as a freak of nature but as a wonder. He dubbed it grano del miracolo—“miracle grain” or “miracle wheat.”

Grossi’s discovery came at just the right time. In Italy in the 1990s, a burgeoning slow-food movement aimed to preserve traditional farming practices and promote natural diets.

Grossi hoped that miracolo could ride this slow-food wave, becoming both a portal to the past and a passage to a future. Perhaps, he thought, miracolo could help other farmers bring back ancient grains, leading the movement that is changing how we make bread, a staple of the human diet. And today, as climate change makes droughts, heat waves and plant disease outbreaks more frequent and intense, a grain that has shown it can fend for itself would help keep that bread on the table.

Farmers began cultivating wheat about 10,000 years ago, in the Fertile Crescent—the area of the Middle East known as the Cradle of Civilization. Thousands of years ago, the hardy and adaptable plant took hold in Europe and Asia. Compared with our modern crops, these ancient wheats were much taller, outperforming other grasses in the field.

Over the millennia, humans bred different varieties of wheat, some yielding less grain and others more. As human populations grew, the strains of wheat that brought plentiful harvests became more desirable. That pattern accelerated amid the upheavals of the early 20th century. By the early 1920s, Italy was still recovering from World War I and unable to grow enough grain to sustain itself; the country was importing roughly a third of its wheat. When fascist leader Benito Mussolini became prime minister in 1922, he launched a campaign to “free the Italian people from the slavery of foreign bread,” by pushing for wheat varieties that yielded greater harvests. The Italian government promoted and planted these “elite” varieties, then distributed the seeds to farmers. Named la Battaglia del Grano, or the Battle of Wheat, this campaign became a global model for agrarian development.

In the United States, wheat harvests were then still plentiful, but not for long: By the early 1930s, amid unprecedented droughts, American farmers found the land was exhausted. The result was the Dust Bowl, during which the previously fertile soils of the Great Plains turned into a desert. American farmers had to look for more drought-resistant varieties that still yielded enough grain.

The midcentury Green Revolution, a movement launched by the American agronomist Norman Borlaug, focused on selective breeding and boosted crop production. This work spread worldwide, feeding countless people. The wheat that was created was indeed more plentiful, yet it came with trade-offs. The petite plants couldn’t always outcompete weeds and were susceptible to disease, so growers used weed killers, fungicides and fertilizer to sustain the crops. Little did they know that these practices would only weaken the health of the soil—while making the wheat even less resilient to changing climate and extreme weather events.

In the 1990s, Grossi sensed that anxiety over wheat harvests was building. That’s why, after he grew wheat from those seeds in the attic, he set out to put the hardy ancient grain back on the table. First, he realized he’d have to solve a big problem: Bread made from the wheat leavened poorly, rising only to fall again. In the early 2000s, he began discussing this challenge with an old local baker who shunned modern machines and still kneaded his dough by hand. The baker was intrigued. The two men started experimenting.

They tried letting the dough rise in smaller batches, using wicker baskets that were taller and helped the dough keep its shape. Soon, the two found another secret: Less kneading made miracolo leaven even better. “The dough was rising, and it was holding its shape,” Grossi says.

One new fan of the bread was Beniamino Perobelli, a student in food science at the University of Parma, who tasted the miracolo bread at a local farmers market and dedicated his undergraduate thesis to investigating its nutritional value. That work bore out what Grossi had already intuited: This wheat was truly ancient—and truly special.

Working with the lab of Teofilo Vamerali, then a professor at the University of Parma, Perobelli determined that the grain was Triticum turgidum—literally “swollen wheat” in Latin. Known in English as “poulard wheat,” it had originally evolved in what today are Turkey, Egypt and other nearby Mediterranean countries. And searching agricultural references, Perobelli found that it had been grown in Italy, too, until farmers shifted toward higher-yield commercial varieties. That solved the mystery of the seed bag stashed away in the attic: It had survived because Grossi’s grandfather saved some of the heritage grains.

The food scientists found that, compared with modern wheats, grano del miracolo was richer in phosphorus and iron. Moreover, to their surprise, they found that T. turgidum had less gluten than modern wheat. And it packed a lot of lysine and tryptophan, the essential amino acids that serve as proteins’ building blocks. It also had more arginine, an amino acid that children need to grow. “The richness of microelements, minerals, and the greater presence of proteins other than gluten were very pleasant surprises,” says Perobelli, now a corporate social responsibility and sustainability manager with Rigoni di Asiago, an Italian company that produces organic fruit spreads, honey and more.

For Grossi, Perobelli’s findings offered scientific proof of his grain’s goodness. He persuaded Molino Grassi, a local organic grain company, to offer the flour to artisanal bakers. Over the next few years, Grossi upped production, so Molino Grassi could sell the flour to restaurants and consumers in Italy and abroad.

By the 2010s, traditional recipes were enjoying a renaissance. So were artisanal bakers and pasta makers, who also became more discerning about which grains they used, says Francesco Sottile, an expert in biodiversity of agrosystems at the University of Palermo.

Ancient grains aren’t necessarily perfect. For example, Grossi has found that miracolo’s height can be a liability—which may be why it fell out of favor with Mussolini. Heavy winds, rains and hail can make the tall stems flip over before the grain ripens, ruining harvests. But Grossi circumvented the problem by planting miracolo with shorter wheat varieties that provide structural support. “I’m quite happy because I developed something that’s like a discovery,” he says.

Relying on a limited number of wheat cultivars, Sottile argues, leaves humanity vulnerable to agricultural disasters: prolonged droughts, extreme heat, new diseases or pests that develop resistance to our chemicals. Diversifying grains reduces the risk—even if some varieties succumb to environmental pressures, others will stand.

Sottile shared an example. “I’m based in Sicily,” he says, where 2024 saw “one of the worst droughts in the last 35 to 40 years.” It was so bad that many commercial wheat growers abandoned their fields in April of that year, realizing they wouldn’t be able to reap the seeds they sowed. Sottile was heartened to see a better fate among smaller-batch farmers who grew heritage grains, more resilient to extreme weather.

“Most of the farmers who were adopting ancient grains, they were able to collect, to harvest,” Sottile says. The world needs more crop biodiversity, he adds—including more ancient grains like grano del miracolo. By the same token, we need more people like Grossi, who, much like the ancient grain he sows, have the tenacity to make a miracle happen.

Stories of gods and grains

“Miracle wheat” is hardly the first divine cereal. Across millennia, gods have taught mortals how to earn their bread

By Sonja Anderson

Greece: While Dionysus provided grapes and Athena was responsible for olives, the goddess Demeter brought grain to the Greeks. In myth, the latter goddess taught farming to a man named Triptolemus (pictured at right), then sent him out on a winged chariot to deliver the knowledge to all of Greece—an episode immortalized on ancient vases.

Mesopotamia: Ancient Sumerians of the Fertile Crescent attributed farming to Ashnan, the grain goddess, “whose face is honey-covered / The lady, the procreatress, the vigor of the land,” per an ancient Sumerian poem. In myth, Ashnan and her sibling Lahar, deity of livestock, once drunkenly debated whether grains or sheep were more important. Enlil and Enki, the paramount Sumerian gods, declared Ashnan the winner, saying that without grain—often fed to herds—there could be no sheep.

Egypt: Osiris ruled over death and the afterlife but was also a god of fertility, and it was said he taught mankind to cultivate wheat. Ancient Egyptians became famously adept at managing this crop: Their growing seasons regularly produced surpluses, thanks to the Nile’s floods. Some priests honored Osiris by planting grain in earthenware shaped like the god.

China: Some ancient Chinese myths trace the country’s agriculture back to one emperor of legend: Shennong, born of a princess and a dragon some 4,000 years ago. The ruler supposedly had a bull’s head and a man’s body and is known as the divine farmer, or emperor of five grains (including rice, millets and wheat). He taught his people how to till their land, expanding the ancient Chinese diet—consisting mainly of meat, clams and wild fruits—to include grains and vegetables.

Mexico: Quetzalcoatl was a deity of the Aztec civilization who, according to myth, created the humans of our current era—the Fifth Sun—and their world. He taught people how to carve rocks, dye cotton, read the stars and—most important—grow food. One day, Quetzalcoatl observed a black ant carrying a kernel of corn, turned himself into an ant and followed the insect through a crack in a stone mountain, where he found a trove of maize, beans, peppers and sage. He took a corn kernel, brought it to man and taught him how to plant it.

item.title: Memdoor: A team of 5 Qwen3.8-27B models beats Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard
item.description:
A multi-agent harness for programming problems, written as a Memdoor workflow. Five roles (planner, two ideators, solver, manager) and a repair worker each start from a fresh context and talk only through files on disk. A shell script that runs the samples decides success, not a model. It is the method of GVS5H (Lee, 2026: five Qwen3.8-27B models match Fable 5 on LiveCodeBench Hard).

Rebuilt with the authors' exact prompts on Qwen3.8-27B, their loop scored a mean of 9.8 of 10 over five passes on the first ten LiveCodeBench Hard problems, against 9.6 for their own harness and 8.0 for Fable 5 alone (below, every run published).

The coder wrote these files itself from a description of the method (2026-10-25). Nobody hand-wrote them.

GVS5H's own harness, rebuilt as a Memdoor workflow on the same model: Qwen3.8-27B, a 128K reply cap, the authors' prompts and loop. The first ten problems of their LiveCodeBench Hard list, five passes, every program graded on every public and hidden test with their corrected grader.

pass Memdoor workflow authors' 27B harness Fable 5 alone 1 10 / 10 9 7 2 10 / 10 10 8 3 10 / 10 10 10 4 10 / 10 9 8 5 9 / 10 10 7 mean 9.8 9.6 8.0

The authors' columns are their repository's regraded result files (q38_multiagent_pN, fable5_single_pN), the numbers in their paper. bench/results/parity-5pass/ holds all 50 runs: every request and reply, the program, the grader's full output, each call's cost and the host that served it, and every attempt that did not count. 49 of 50 solved; the 50 runs cost $35.79 (15.3M output tokens), $38.77 with the 16 attempts that were cut by a clock, stopped for a fix or paused.

Note: ten problems, five passes each, not the authors' 100. The contests date from 29 March to 6 April 2025, and the model may have seen them in training: contamination cannot be ruled out. Fable 5's column is a single call per problem from the authors' files; it was not run in this harness. The loop sees only the public samples; the score is the hidden tests. A run took a median of 40 minutes of model time (the longest 4 hours) and $0.39. All on OpenRouter, not a local machine; Modal does not publish its precision. Local paths in the run scripts and in four tracebacks a manager was shown read <scratch> and $HOME; nothing else in the runs is edited.

Same as the authors'. Every message, byte for byte: lib/test_parity.py runs their multiagent_solve and our workflow against one scripted model and compares each request (four cases, all identical; a one-character change makes them differ). The temperatures (plan 0.3, ideation 0.4, manager and worker 0.2), top_p 0.95 and top_k 20 (what their vLLM applied from the model's own config), the 128K cap, up to 10 rounds, a cut-off worker summarized, and a reply with no text answered by its reasoning.

Different. The host. Theirs was their own vLLM in FP8. Ours is OpenRouter, asked in the order Modal, CoreWeave, Parasail, Wafer until Modal slowed to 14 tokens/s, then the FP8 hosts only (Wafer, Parasail, CoreWeave): 203 calls were served by Modal, 27 by CoreWeave and 115 by Wafer, every one of the FP8 order's calls by Wafer. Three runs were moved mid-run, their finished steps kept (log/host-switch.txt).

What it took. The problem text was the mismatch: our first version wrote its own task file around each problem, and the 27B planned worse from it than from the authors' exact LiveCodeBench text (arc196_c's plan: 0 of 2 against 2 of 2). Four Memdoor changes let a workflow ask what their harness asks: a task answers with the model's reasoning when it wrote no text, top_p/top_k on a model line, mark_cutoff for a reply cut at the cap, and a call that runs on its own four-hour clock.

Where it lost. Twice, the same two gaps in the authors' loop:

Pass 5, abc399_e (32 of 44 hidden): round 1's program was right; the manager invented a counterexample with a wrong expected answer, the team rewrote it, and the new program passed the samples, which do not cover the case. Pass 4, arc196_c and arc196_d: a program passing every hidden test was overwritten by a later round because the manager did not say done; both got a correct program back before the loop's end (arc196_d at round 8, arc196_c through the final call), at $3.44 and $4.24, the two most expensive runs.

Both are fixable without changing the method (check a manager's counterexample against a brute force on small inputs; keep the last program that passed the samples). Neither is in these numbers.

curl -fsSL https://memdoor.ai/install.sh | bash memdoor connect openrouter # or anthropic, openai, gemini, chatgpt git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/guregodevo/memdoor mkdir -p ~/.memdoor/workflows cp -r memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve ~/.memdoor/workflows/ # the library: any project sees it mkdir my-problem && cd my-problem cp -r ../memdoor/examples/workflows/team-solve/sample/* . # task.md + tests/1.in … 5.out memdoor workflow run team-solve --wait # progress on stderr, exit 0 when every sample passes

/workflow in memdoor tui draws the same run live. For your own problem, replace task.md and put paired tests/N.in / tests/N.out files beside it. The program is solution.py, read from stdin, compared to the samples with diff. It needs Python 3 and bash. To keep it with one repo instead, copy the folder into that project's .memdoor/workflows/. The project's copy wins.

The steps name no model. Whatever /model is pinned to answers, a local one included (memdoor connect local for janis, Ollama or llama-server).

plan ──┬── ideate-a ──┬── solve ── test ── review ── repair ── verify └── ideate-b ──┘ step kind reads writes plan agent task.md plan.md, and a notes.md ledger with one anchor per ideator ideate-a, ideate-b agent, in parallel task.md, plan.md, notes.md a proposal at its own anchor: A the most direct provable algorithm, B one from a different family of technique solve agent both proposals the decision in notes.md, solution.py test command tests/ test-output.log, test-status.txt (never fails the run) review agent the captured test output, not a model's claim review.md, repair instructions in notes.md repair agent the manager's instructions a fixed solution.py, or nothing if the samples passed verify command tests/ final-test-output.log; nonzero exit fails the run

Every agent prompt says "fresh context, read the files, do not rely on chat". The paper credits that ledger discipline for the gain. There is one repair round and no human gate. The last step is the whole verdict:

type: command requires: - table_pattern: repair command: | check=.memdoor/workflows/team-solve/check-samples.sh [ -f "$check" ] || check="$HOME/.memdoor/workflows/team-solve/check-samples.sh" bash "$check" > final-test-output.log 2>&1 result=$? cat final-test-output.log exit "$result"

Each step is one YAML file in steps/, the format of mario, the engine underneath. requires: is the DAG. Changing a role means changing its prompt.

The sample: count the substrings of a string over {a, b, c} with equal counts of each letter, up to 200,000 characters. Run on the default ladder through OpenRouter:

8 of 8 steps, 5 of 5 samples. The solver took ideator A's prefix-state method, O(N) with a dictionary of (a−b, a−c) pairs. A brute force on 300 random strings found no mismatch afterwards, and it runs in 0.04 s at N = 200,000. The manager found nothing to repair. One ideator's provider dropped the stream mid-answer. The coder had written max_retries: 0, so the run died there. The agent steps now carry max_retries: 1, and the run was resumed with --partition, which kept the planner's and the other ideator's work. The ideator prompts the coder wrote named the sample's methods (A: a streaming prefix-state count, B: sorting prefix states), which would steer any other problem the wrong way. They now ask A for the most direct provable algorithm and B for one from a different family of technique (2026-10-28). The first attempts failed every step in 0 s with "no agent named coder": a run looked its agent up only in its own workspace. That was fixed in the gateway the same day (v1.692.0).

item.title: When Electric Cars Were for Women
item.description:
At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Who Invented the Mercury-Arc Rectifier?

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

A Carriage Maker Pivots to Electric Cars

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Thomas Edison Designed a Bad Battery

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

We’re Charging Our Cars Wrong › False Starts: The Story of Vehicle-to-Grid Power › This Power Grid Pioneer’s EV Prediction Came 100 Years Too Soon ›

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.
